newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Oil markets weaker as more Iraqi exports loom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Oil markets weaker as more Iraqi exports loom.

text.p: World oil markets fell on Tuesday amid reports that the United Nations was likely to extend its "oil-for-food" deal with Iraq and jitters ahead of the release of weekly U.S. stocks data.
Members of the Security Council were scheduled to meet on Tuesday to draft a resolution allowing Iraq to sell another $2 billion worth of oil over the next six months.
"The indications are that it will get the go-ahead this week... There is a formal meeting (of the Security Council) tentatively scheduled for Friday," said a U.N. source.
A vote could be taken as early as Wednesday, officials said.
Brent Blend crude, the world benchmark grade, closed 62 cents down at $18.90 a barrel in London. It has averaged $19.39 in the past four months.
But while the prospect of fresh Iraqi exports was providing a bearish backdrop to the market, dealers had been expecting the deal to be renewed.
The rollover of the Iraqi deal is "already built into the market," said Bob Finch, head trader at Vitol SA, the world's largest independent oil trading and refining company.
The only uncertainty had been whether the United States would approve an extension of the plan and that disappeared on Tuesday when the State Department pledged its support.
"The Secretary (of State) has decided that the United States will support the renewal of U.N. Resolution 986 and that is the oil for food deal," spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
The deal, an exception to the economic sanctions in place since Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990, expires on June 7.
Under its terms, Baghdad was allowed to use oil earnings to buy food, medicines and other necessities for ordinary Iraqis who have suffered under the sanctions regime.
The release of weekly U.S. stocks data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) after the close of trade on Tuesday was a more immediate attention grabber, traders said.
Oil markets have been volatile in recent weeks and dealers are waiting to see if the normal seasonal pickup in gasoline demand in the United States will be enough to underpin prices.
U.S. crude stocks, which have been running 18 million barrels above year-ago levels, will also be watched with interest.
"There's no urge to move out of the current price range," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of the oil division at Bankers Trust International in London.
"Fundamentally there's too much oil around but frankly there always is at this time of year," he added.
Despite an overhang of prompt oil, due in part to overproduction by OPEC, the forward outlook is more balanced with winter demand likely to mop up unsold barrels, according to traders.
Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer and OPEC heavyweight, expects rising world oil demand to keep crude prices buoyant for the remainder of the year, a Gulf source said recently.
The source, familiar with oil policy in the kingdom, said Saudi expectations for demand on Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries crude this year had been revised higher.
Saudi Arabia saw demand on OPEC oil at around 27 million barrels a day (bpd) on average this year compared to a previous projection of 26.3 million bpd made at the end of 1996.
For the second year running, analysts have cut their forecasts for non-OPEC supply growth because new North Sea fields have failed to come on stream when planned.
On Friday the International Energy Agency in Paris, the West's oil watchdog, is due to release figures estimating global oil demand for next winter and beyond.
